5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Building on the ownership/transfer framing from colleagues 2, 5, 8, 9, 13 and 14, I continue to see D as the stronger classification. The phrase does not merely reify love as an isolated physical object; it imposes the full relational logic of a resource that can be possessed, quantified, allocated or directed (“my” + “for humanity”), allowing systematic inference about how much affection one “has” and where it is channeled. That is precisely the cross-domain structuring Lakoff & Johnson highlight when they illustrate structural metaphors, whereas the ontological/physical label tends to cover simpler substance or container cases without this inferential payoff. The paper’s own examples of everyday emotion language repeatedly show possession schemas organizing reasoning in exactly this way, so treating the example as merely “physical” risks under-describing the mapping at work. If the taxonomy permits overlap, the richer structural reading better captures why the expression feels productive.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Building directly on the ownership-and-transfer points raised by colleagues 2, 5, 8, 9, 13 and 14, the expression “my love for humanity” supplies a systematic relational structure that goes beyond bare entity reification. It imports the full inferential logic of property schemas—possessor, quantifiable resource, directed allocation (“for”)—so that one can reason about how much affection is “held,” whether it can be “given,” and to whom it is apportioned. Lakoff & Johnson repeatedly illustrate structural metaphors precisely by showing how such everyday possession and transfer relations organize an abstract domain; the ontological label alone does not capture that cross-domain productivity. This framing also explains why purely spatial or generic superordinate readings fall short here and why the example continues to support productive inferences in ordinary discourse.
